toolCalls.name: StructuredOutput

output.brief:
The problem is concentrated in the Kestrel team, not in the group's pay or the firm-wide hours target. Eight of the 11 associates on Kestrel have resigned, against one of the 13 who were never on it. Other groups' attrition is flat, which rules out a firm-wide cause. Pay is in line with the rest of the firm, and the rival firm's premium is £3–5k, not the £15k quoted. Most leavers took equal or lower pay. A retention payment would therefore spend £228k on a cause that the evidence doesn't support, and closing the review would stop the search for the real one.

What the evidence can't separate is the Kestrel workload from Dorian Faulk's supervision. All 11 Kestrel associates report to him, and he supervises on no other matter. The survey comments point to both: months of weekend work and humiliating late-night corrections. Kestrel staff were also picked for low utilisation, so selection is a possible confounder.

Next step: don't announce the payment. Commission the roughly £9k confidential external interviews, designed to separate supervision from workload. Add matter and supervisor fields to attrition reporting. Hold the supervision change and the contract reviewers until the interviews report, with a check on any further resignations in the meantime. I'm fairly sure about what to rule out and uncertain about which of the two causes dominates.
